content: const total = items.reduce((acc, item) => acc + item.price, 0);
explanation: reduce walks the array carrying a running value. The 0 is the starting total; drop it and an empty array throws.

content: const unique = [...new Set(values)].sort((a, b) => a - b);
explanation: A Set discards duplicates. Spreading it back to an array allows sorting; the comparator is required or numbers sort as text.

content: export async function load(url) { const res = await fetch(url); return res.json(); }
explanation: fetch resolves as soon as headers arrive, so .json() is a second await for the body. It does not throw on a 404 - check res.ok.

content: document.querySelectorAll('.row').forEach(el => el.classList.toggle('active'));
explanation: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList, so it will not change as you mutate the elements in it.

content: if (typeof value !== 'string' || value.length === 0) { return null; }
explanation: A guard clause: reject the bad input first and return, instead of nesting the real work inside an if.

content: const { id, name = 'anonymous', ...rest } = await request.json();
explanation: Destructuring with a default and a rest property. The default applies only when the value is undefined, not when it is null.

content: squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 21) if n % 3 != 0]
explanation: A list comprehension: the expression, the loop, then the filter. Faster and clearer than appending in a for loop.

content: def fib(n): return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
explanation: Recursion with a base case. Correct but exponential - each call spawns two more, so it recomputes the same values repeatedly.

content: with open('data.csv', encoding='utf-8') as f: rows = [line.split(',') for line in f]
explanation: with closes the file even if the body raises. Iterating a file yields lines without loading it all into memory.

content: counts = {word: text.count(word) for word in set(text.split())}
explanation: A dict comprehension. Note it is quadratic: count rescans the whole string per word. collections.Counter is the right tool.

content: try: value = int(raw) except ValueError: value = 0
explanation: Catching the specific exception, not a bare except - a bare one would also swallow KeyboardInterrupt.

content: let mut counts: HashMap<String, usize> = HashMap::new();
explanation: mut because inserting mutates it. The type annotation is needed here since nothing yet tells the compiler what it holds.

content: fn main() { println!("{}", args().skip(1).collect::<Vec<_>>().join(" ")); }
explanation: skip(1) drops the program name, which is always the first argument. Vec<_> lets the compiler infer the element type.

content: let total: i64 = values.iter().filter(|v| **v > 0).sum();
explanation: iter() borrows rather than consuming. The double deref is because filter hands you a reference to the iterator's own reference.

content: match result { Ok(v) => println!("{v}"), Err(e) => eprintln!("error: {e}") }
explanation: match on a Result must cover both arms - the compiler rejects it otherwise, which is how Rust stops an error going unhandled.

content: pub struct Point { pub x: f64, pub y: f64 }
explanation: Fields are private by default in Rust, so each one needs its own pub - making the struct public does not publish its contents.

content: impl Display for Token { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter) -> Result { write!(f, "{}", self.0) } }
explanation: Implementing Display is what makes a type usable in {}. self.0 is the first field of a tuple struct.

content: int *buf = malloc(len * sizeof(int)); if (!buf) return -1;
explanation: malloc returns NULL when it fails, and checking is not optional. sizeof(int) rather than 4 keeps it correct across platforms.

content: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { sum += a[i] * b[i]; }
explanation: A dot product. The bound is < n, not <= n; off-by-one here reads past the end of the array.

content: struct node { int value; struct node *next; };
explanation: A linked-list node. It refers to its own type through a pointer, which is legal because a pointer has a known size.

content: for i, v := range items { fmt.Printf("%d: %v\n", i, v) }
explanation: range yields index and value. In Go before 1.22 the loop variable was reused each iteration, which surprised anyone capturing it in a closure.

content: if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("read config: %w", err) }
explanation: Go's error convention. %w wraps the original so errors.Is and errors.As can still see it further up.

content: public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("ready"); }
explanation: Java's entry point. The signature is fixed: static so it runs without an instance, and taking the command-line arguments.

content: grep -rn "TODO" src/ | awk -F: '{print $1}' | sort -u
explanation: grep -n prints file:line:text, awk splits on the colon to take the filename, sort -u removes the duplicates.

content: for f in *.log; do gzip -9 "$f" && echo "packed $f"; done
explanation: The quotes around $f matter: without them a filename containing a space becomes two arguments.

content: export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" && command -v rg >/dev/null || echo missing
explanation: Prepending puts your own binaries ahead of the system ones. command -v is the portable test for whether something is installed.
Finds the commit that introduced a bug by bisecting history. Give it a known-good and known-bad commit and it halves the range each step.
content: git bisect start HEAD v1.2.0 && git bisect run ./test.sh

explanation: Who last touched each line of a range, which is how you find the person to ask rather than the person to blame.
content: git log -L 40,60:src/parser.rs --oneline

explanation: Recovers commits that are no longer reachable from any branch. A hard reset does not destroy them; it just stops pointing at them.
content: git reflog --date=iso | head -20

explanation: zip pairs two sequences and stops at the shorter one. strict=True makes a length mismatch an error rather than silent truncation.
content: for name, score in zip(names, scores, strict=True): print(f'{name}: {score:>5.1f}')

explanation: defaultdict removes the exists-check before every append, which is the most common shape of a grouping loop.
content: groups = defaultdict(list); [groups[w[0]].append(w) for w in words]

explanation: ?? falls back only on null or undefined, unlike ||, which also fires on 0 and the empty string.
content: const port = config.port ?? process.env.PORT ?? 8080;

explanation: Promise.all runs them concurrently and rejects on the first failure; allSettled waits for every result instead.
content: const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([getUser(id), getPosts(id)]);

explanation: The ? operator returns early on Err, converting the error type through From. It is what keeps error handling from nesting.
content: let config: Config = toml::from_str(&fs::read_to_string(path)?)?;

explanation: entry().or_insert_with() looks the key up once. The obvious contains_key-then-insert hashes it twice.
content: *counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;

explanation: A window function ranks rows within each partition without collapsing them, which a GROUP BY cannot do.
content: SELECT user_id, wpm, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY mode ORDER BY wpm DESC) AS rank FROM results;

explanation: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and reports what the planner actually did, not what it guessed it would do.
content: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM test_results WHERE mode_key = 'time-30' ORDER BY wpm DESC LIMIT 50;
const grouped = items.reduce((acc, item) => ({ ...acc, [item.type]: [...(acc[item.type] ?? []), item] }), {});
explanation: Groups a list by one field. The nullish coalescing operator supplies an empty array the first time a type is seen, so no separate initialisation step is needed.

content: let counts: HashMap<&str, usize> = text.split_whitespace().fold(HashMap::new(), |mut m, w| { *m.entry(w).or_insert(0) += 1; m });
explanation: entry returns a view into the slot for a key whether or not it exists. or_insert fills it on first sight, and the star dereferences that slot so it can be incremented in place.

content: with open(path, encoding='utf-8') as fh: rows = [line.rstrip('\n').split('\t') for line in fh if line.strip()]
explanation: The with block closes the file even if the loop raises. Naming the encoding matters: without it Python uses the machine's locale, so the same file can parse differently elsewhere.

content: impl fmt::Display for Error { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result { write!(f, "{}: {}", self.kind, self.detail) } }
explanation: Implementing Display is what lets a type be printed with the plain brace form. The formatter carries the width and precision the caller asked for.

content: export const debounce = (fn, ms) => { let t; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); }; };
explanation: The timer handle lives in the closure, so every returned function keeps its own. Each call cancels the pending one, and only a pause longer than ms lets the work through.

content: SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id GROUP BY u.id, u.name HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 5;
explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps users with no orders, and HAVING filters on the aggregate, which WHERE cannot do because WHERE runs before the grouping.

content: def chunked(seq, n): return [seq[i:i + n] for i in range(0, len(seq), n)]
explanation: Slicing past the end of a sequence is not an error in Python, it simply returns what is there, so the final chunk needs no special case.

content: match value { Some(n) if n > 0 => n, Some(_) => 0, None => return Err(Error::Missing) }
explanation: The if after a pattern is a match guard. It narrows an arm without a nested conditional, and the compiler still checks that every case is covered.

content: const sorted = [...items].sort((a, b) => a.score - b.score || a.name.localeCompare(b.name));
explanation: sort mutates, so the spread makes a copy first. The logical or supplies a second comparison used only when the scores are equal.

content: async fn fetch_all(urls: Vec<String>) -> Vec<Result<String, Error>> { futures::future::join_all(urls.into_iter().map(fetch)).await }
explanation: join_all drives every future at once on one task and waits for all of them, rather than awaiting each in turn, which would make the requests sequential.
